title: The siege
hook: grievances grow, rebels surround his house, and he refuses to let blood be shed for him

segments.voice: Yesterday: mushaf. Hafsah's sheets became Zayd's copies, one for each province. Your line was one text for all.

The street outside the caliph's house is full of armed men, and they are not foreign soldiers. They are Muslims, from Egypt and the garrison towns of Iraq, with complaints about governors, appointments and money. They have camped in Medina, and they want Uthman to step down. He will not take off what God has put on him, he says. So they close in on his house. Inside are a few companions and young men, among them, the histories say, Hasan, the Prophet's grandson, sent by Ali to guard the door. They have swords. And the old man inside tells them to put the swords away.
screen: `ARMED MEN IN THE STREET.` → `STEP DOWN, THEY SAY.` → `PUT THE SWORDS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Fitnah. In the Qur'an the word carries trial, temptation and testing, and the lexicons connect the root with smelting gold in fire to see what is real. Later Muslims also use it for civil strife, Muslim against Muslim, a test of a different kind. The histories give the name to the years that begin at Uthman's door. Why did he refuse a defense? The sources point back to the Prophet. Bukhari records a day when the Prophet sat at a well and the companions came one by one asking to enter. For Abu Bakr: give him the good news of paradise. For Umar, the same. For Uthman: the good news of paradise, with a trial that will befall him. Uthman answered, the report says: God is the one whose help is sought. And Tirmidhi records the Prophet telling Uthman that God might clothe him in a shirt, and if people wanted him to take it off, he should not. Uthman read these as a calling: keep the office, and don't let Muslims kill Muslims to save his life. So, the histories report, he told those guarding him to go home, and told the servants who would fight that whoever laid down his weapon was free. Readers have argued ever since. Holiness, or handing the city to the rebels? Sunni tradition honors it as the restraint of a martyr. Shia tellings put the weight on the grievances he had not answered. The sources agree on the core: he forbade fighting for him.
screen: `FITNAH: TRIAL BY FIRE.` · `PARADISE, WITH A TRIAL.` · `DO NOT TAKE OFF THE SHIRT.` · `GO HOME. LAY DOWN YOUR WEAPON.` · then, large: `HE FORBADE FIGHTING FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one live conflict: a family thread, a neighbor, a coworker, a comment section. Find the move you've been tempted to make, the reply that would bring in your allies, and set it down, without giving up what's right. If you pray, you can ask for help in the trial.
Fitnah. Trial and testing in the Qur'an, and later the name for strife among Muslims, beginning, the histories say, with the siege of Uthman's house. Today's word.
Your line: he forbade fighting for him. Restraint can be its own kind of courage. That's day eight hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: The histories name the siege of Uthman as the start of the fitnah; Sunni teachers cite his refusal to let Muslims fight on his behalf, and Shia tellings put the weight on the grievances behind the revolt.

notes: Audit: read in full; no changes. Lane's f-t-n entry and Bukhari 3695 ('God is the one whose help is sought') match the script.

Hasan guarding the door, the freeing of servants who laid down arms, and Uthman's refusal to step down are from the histories (al-Tabari and others); confirm phrasing.
